evidence.quote:
Route 52 crosses Walker Mountain passing by Big Walker Lookout at the crest.

evidence.claim: Big Walker Mountain Scenic Byway crosses the mountain through Jefferson National Forest on State Highway 717 and US 52/21.
evidence.quote: the Big Walker Mountain Scenic Byway traverses 16.2 miles of State Highway 717 and US 52/21 in the Jefferson National Forest.

evidence.claim: The National Forest Scenic Byway runs 16.2 miles; America’s Scenic Byways suggests allowing about 30 minutes.
evidence.quote: 16.2 miles - Allow about 30 minutes.

evidence.claim: The National Forest Scenic Byway
evidence.quote: National Forest Scenic Byway

evidence.claim: Its account emphasizes overlooks across the Ridge and Valley landscape, with Mount Rogers visible from the mountain top.
evidence.quote: Overlooks provide views of the Ridge and Valley landscape of the region. Views from the top of Big Walker Mountain stretch for many miles and include a view of Mount Rogers, the highest peak in Virginia.

evidence.claim: Interstate 77 passes beneath the mountain in a tunnel, while Route 52 crosses its crest.
evidence.quote:
Route 52 crosses Walker Mountain passing by Big Walker Lookout at the crest.  
Interstate I-77 passes under Walker Mountain in Big Walker Mountain Tunnel.

evidence.claim: The byway account describes spring blooms of rhododendron, azalea and mountain laurel, with red and gold foliage in autumn.
evidence.quote: Rhododendron, azalea and mountain laurel all bloom in profusion each spring. Fiery reds and golds surround this scenic journey each autumn.

evidence.claim: The crossing also figures in the story of the 1863 Wytheville raid.
evidence.quote: Historically speaking, the scenic byway over Big Walker Mountain is the route traversed during the Civil War by Mary "Molly" Tynes

evidence.claim: Local legend credits Molly Tynes with riding through the mountains to warn Wytheville of approaching Union horsemen.
evidence.quote: Local legend says that on July 17, a farmer in Tazewell County (located north of Wytheville) sent his daughter on a night ride to warn the town of Wytheville of the approaching Union horsemen. The young woman, Molly Tynes, rode 41 mi (66.0 km) through mountain ranges and a forest to warn the small town.

evidence.claim: The Union expedition targeted the Virginia & Tennessee Railroad and its telegraph line.
evidence.quote: Their orders, which came from General Eliakim P. Scammon, were to disable the Virginia & Tennessee Railroad. Telegraph line strung along the railroad line was also a target.

evidence.claim: The raiders occupied the town, but the railroad damage was repaired in less than an hour.
evidence.quote: A small amount of damage was inflicted on the railroad line, but it was later repaired in less than an hour.

evidence.claim: The raiders occupied the town
evidence.quote: Despite significant losses, the Union brigade was eventually able to secure the town.

evidence.quote: Route 52 crosses Walker Mountain passing by Big Walker Lookout at the crest.

evidence.claim: Bland was first known as Bland Court House, a name that fits the reason its county was created.
evidence.quote: Bland was originally known as Bland Court House.

evidence.claim: Residents faced long journeys and difficult mountain trails to conduct legal business at the existing county seats.
evidence.quote: The distances and the difficult mountain trails created a significant hardship for those needing to conduct legal affairs.

evidence.claim: They also objected to paying taxes for benefits outside their area.
evidence.quote: the growing population resented paying taxes for benefits outside of the local area.

evidence.claim: That pressure persuaded the General Assembly to create a new county in 1861 from parts of Wythe, Tazewell and Giles counties.
evidence.quote:
This pressure eventually persuaded the Virginia General Assembly to take action to form a new county in the southwestern portion of the state.
Bland County was officially formed on March 30, 1861, from parts of Wythe, Tazewell, and Giles counties.

evidence.claim: Bland remains the county seat, in a county of mountains and small river valleys.
evidence.quote: The county seat is the unincorporated area of Bland.

evidence.claim: in a county of mountains and small river valleys
evidence.quote: The county is mountainous with small river valleys running through the county.

evidence.claim: The county took its name from Richard Bland, a Virginia statesman who served in the House of Burgesses and Continental Congress.
evidence.quote: The new county was named in honor of Richard Bland, a Virginia statesman who served in the House of Burgesses and the Continental Congress.

evidence.claim: Big Walker Lookout adds a 100-foot observation tower to the mountain crest.
evidence.quote: Big Walker Lookout is a 100 feet (30 m) observation tower located in the Blue Ridge Highlands Region atop Big Walker Mountain

evidence.claim: Built in 1947, it has been operated continuously by the Kime family.
evidence.quote: The tower was originally built in 1947 and has been run continuously by the Kime family.

evidence.claim: The lookout’s listed elevation is 3,405 feet, and its view takes in mountain peaks in five states.
evidence.quote: Located at an elevation of 3,405 feet (1,038 m), the view from the top of the tower encompasses mountain peaks in five different states.

evidence.claim: The approach has changed: the original general store burned in 2003 and a replacement was built beside it.
evidence.quote: The first store building burned in 2003 and a new store was built just to the right of the first.

evidence.claim: The swinging bridge once used to reach the tower survived the fire; it leads to the edge where the old staircase connected.
evidence.quote: The swinging bridge was not destroyed in the fire and still stands. Visitors can cross to the edge where the original staircase connected to the bridge.

evidence.claim: Seasonal raptor migrations are another feature of the ridge: birds of prey use rising warm air from the valley to conserve energy.
evidence.quote: Birds of prey use the warm air rising from the valley floor to conserve their energy while migrating.

evidence.claim: The swinging bridge survived the fire that destroyed the original store.
evidence.quote: The swinging bridge was not destroyed in the fire and still stands.

evidence.claim: Wytheville carried the name Evansham until a fire in March 1839, after which it was renamed.
evidence.quote: in October 1792, the town was officially named Evansham, for prominent local citizen Jesse Evans. After a disastrous fire in March 1839, the town was renamed Wytheville.

evidence.claim: The Haller–Gibboney Rock House predates that change: its two-story limestone dwelling was built in 1822–1823.
evidence.quote: It was built in 1822–1823, and is a two-story, five bay late Federal style limestone dwelling.

evidence.claim: During the Civil War battle at Wytheville, the house served as a hospital.
evidence.quote: The Rock House was used as a hospital during the Battle of Wytheville during Civil War.

evidence.claim: The building now houses a museum sponsored by the Wythe County Historical Society.
evidence.quote: The building houses a museum sponsored by the Wythe County Historical Society.

evidence.claim: Its late Federal design includes a side-gabled roof and a frame wing ending in a half-octagon.
evidence.quote: It has a side gable roof and a two-story frame ell terminating in a demi-octagonal end.

evidence.claim: The Rock House belongs to the town’s historic district but has its own National Register listing, dating to 1972.
evidence.quote: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1972.

evidence.claim: The Rock House belongs to the town’s historic district but has its own National Register listing
evidence.quote: The Haller-Gibboney Rock House and St. John's Episcopal Church are located in the district and listed separately.

flags: The cached byway page supports National Forest Scenic Byway status but not the catalog’s 1989 date; omitted the date. Published byway length is 16.2 miles, whereas the material strip connecting Bland and Wytheville is 22 miles.

No construction history is cached. The route history uses the documented raid association; Molly Tynes’s ride remains explicitly a local legend, following the detailed raid account. The tourism account’s claim of repulsing the Union force conflicts with the raid account’s occupation of town; omitted that claim.
Dropped the current Bland population of 312: both cached Bland pages give 383 for 2020.
The lookout access information is from Wikipedia, not its operator. No current hours, admission amount or guaranteed access supplied.
